4-2-kiloyear-event: The 4.2-kiloyear event was an aridification, a long-term drought, 4,200 years ago, and one of the most severe climatic events of the Holocene. It most likely lasted the whole 22nd century BCE. In 2018 the International Commission on Stratigraphy designated the late Holocene, from around 2250 BCE, the Meghalayan age, with a stalagmite in Mawmluh cave in India as its boundary stratotype. The division is debated, since the event was not a global drought and fell within no clear timeframe.

Modelling suggests a significant weakening of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation disrupted ocean currents and moved the Intertropical Convergence Zone southward, and more variable El Niño–Southern Oscillation conditions may also have played a part.

Evidence of intense aridity around 2200 BCE comes from North Africa, the Middle East, the Arabian Peninsula, the Indian subcontinent and North America. The effects were uneven: northern Poland became drier, the Alps wetter, and no signal has been found at Rodrigues. In Egypt a series of exceptionally low Nile floods around 2150 BCE may have contributed to the end of the Old Kingdom's central government after a famine.

In Mesopotamia archaeology records widespread abandonment of the northern plains and an influx of refugees into the south around 2170 BCE. A 180-kilometre wall, the Repeller of the Amorites, was built across central Mesopotamia against nomadic incursions, and around 2150 BCE the Gutian people from the Zagros Mountains defeated the Akkadian army.

The event has been hypothesised to have caused the collapse of the Old Kingdom in Egypt, the Akkadian Empire and the Liangzhu culture, and to have begun the decline of the Indus Valley Civilisation, whose people moved south-east. Some scientists disagree, since the drought was not global.

In China a weakened East Asian Summer Monsoon left a humidity gradient between north and south. The Longshan culture of the Yishu River Basin lost population and sites and was displaced around 2000 BCE by the Yueshi culture, while Longshan in the less affected Luoyang Basin continued to thrive. Resettlement of northern Mesopotamia by smaller sedentary populations came near 1900 BCE, three centuries after the collapse.
